questions.question: A proposed bonus-malus scheme lists its rating levels and initial level and specifies an update for every current level and annual reported count. Given a base premium, which missing component prevents calculation of prices at its levels?
options: The realised claim count from the coming year.
The monetary size of every future claim.
A premium relativity for each level.
The individual Poisson claim-frequency parameter of each policy.

questions.question: Two policies have the same initial rating factors but different reported claim histories. Why can a bonus-malus system later charge different premiums?
options: It directly observes each policyholder's true latent risk rate.
It uses observed experience to update their rating levels.
It guarantees every policyholder pays the same lifetime premium.
It discards initial rating factors and prices only claim severity.

questions.question: A bonus-malus update is $L_{t+1}=T(L_t,N_t)$, where $L_t$ is current level and $N_t$ the reported count in year $t$. For two policies with the same current level and count but different claim amounts, what must their next levels be?
options: The same under this stated count-only rule.
Different whenever total claim amounts differ.
The same only if their claim sizes are independent.
Different whenever their unobserved individual risk rates differ.

questions.question: In a bonus-malus model, $N_t\mid\Lambda=\lambda\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$, where $N_t$ is annual count and $\Lambda$ a policyholder's unobserved risk rate. What is conditioned on in this statement?
options: The event that the annual count is positive.
The population average $\mathbb{E}[\Lambda]$ substituted for every individual.
A fixed value $\lambda$ of the individual risk rate.
The current rating level $L_t$ interpreted as the annual risk parameter.

questions.question: A bonus-malus level has relativity $0.8$ and the base premium is 120 euros. What premium does this level charge?
options: 120.8 euros.
96 euros.
150 euros.
24 euros.

questions.question: A two-level bonus-malus scheme charges 100 euros in level A and 200 euros in level B. A new policy enters A in year 1; any reported claim moves it to B for the following year. It reports one claim during year 1. Which premiums apply in years 1 and 2 respectively?
options: 100 euros and 200 euros.
200 euros and 200 euros.
100 euros and 100 euros.
200 euros and 100 euros.

questions.question: A bonus-malus rule charges the lower premium next year exactly when the current reported count $N$ is zero. For a fixed individual risk $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(1)$, what is the probability of qualifying for that lower price?

A bonus-malus system has base premium $c>0$ and levels labelled 1 and 2 with relativities $r_1=2$ and $r_2=0.8$. A reported claim changes level1 to level2. Which interpretation is justified by these prices?
options: It reduces the charged premium despite increasing the level label.
It raises the charged premium because the level label increases.
It leaves the premium unchanged because the base stays fixed.
It proves the underlying individual risk rate has fallen.

questions.question: Every level $l$ charges $c r_l$, where $c>0$ is a base premium and $r_l>0$ a relativity. Replace the base by $a c$ and every relativity by $r_l/a$ for a fixed $a>0$, keeping all level updates unchanged. Which statement about charged prices holds for every such scheme and positive scale?
options: Every price is multiplied by a.
No charged price changes.
Every price is divided by a.
All price differences disappear.

questions.question: A policy’s relativity falls from 1 to 0.8 next year, while its base premium rises from 100 to 150 euros. Does the lower relativity alone guarantee a lower charged premium under the bonus-malus pricing rule?
options: Yes; a lower relativity always reduces the monetary premium across years.
Yes; the relativity reduction leaves the next premium at 80 euros.
No; the changed base makes the next premium 150 euros.
No; the next premium is 120 euros, exceeding the original 100 euros.

questions.question: A two-year history scheme has states G (claim last year), P (no claim last year but a claim the year before), and I (no claims in the last two years). G and P charge 200 euros; I charges 100 euros. A policy starts in P, then reports zero claims in year1 and one claim in year2. Which states follow those years?
options: G then I.
P then G.
I then G.
I then P.

questions.question: A policy has three loss incidents this year, but only one claim is reported. Its current bonus-malus level is 2 and its count-based update is $T(l,n)=\min(l+n,4)$ for reported count $n$ and levels $1,2,3,4$. What next level follows from the supplied observed history?

For a fixed-risk policy, annual count $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(1)$. A fully specified one-year bonus-malus rule charges 100 euros next year if $N=0$ and 200 euros otherwise. What is the expected next-year charged premium?
options: $200-100\mathrm{e}^{-1}$ euros.
$100+100\mathrm{e}^{-1}$ euros.
$200\mathrm{e}^{-1}$ euros.
$100(1-\mathrm{e}^{-1})$ euros.

questions.question: A scheme charges $a<c$ after two consecutive claim-free years, and $c$ otherwise. One policy claimed last year; another was claim-free last year but claimed the year before. Both currently pay $c$. If the next year is claim-free, why can their current price alone not determine the next price?
options: The first still pays $c$; the second earns $a$.
Both must pay $a$ because the new year is claim-free.
Both must pay $c$ because their current prices coincide.
The first earns $a$; the second still pays $c$.

questions.question: Let one random count $Z\sim\operatorname{Pois}(1)$ be used every year: $N_0=N_1=N_2=Z$. A two-level update starts at $L_0=0$ and sets $L_{t+1}$ to the remainder of $L_t+N_t$ on division by 2. Each annual count has the required Poisson marginal. Since $L_2=0$ always, does that current level alone determine the conditional law of $L_3$ when older level $L_1$ is known?
options: Yes; $L_3=0$ in every history because $L_2=0$.
No; $L_3=L_1$, so older level history remains relevant.
Yes; annual Poisson marginals make the counts independent.
No; the rule fails to map into its two available levels.

questions.question: A fixed latent risk rate $\Lambda$ is equally likely to be $\log2$ or $\log4$. Given that rate, yearly reported counts are independent Poisson variables. A scheme charges its low current price when last year had zero reports. Compare the probability of zero reports next year given two most recent years were zero, with that given only last year was zero. What are the respective probabilities?

Two bonus-malus levels charge 100 and 150 euros, respectively, using one unknown base premium $c>0$. Their unknown relativities must each lie in $[0.5,1.5]$ and the price at a level is base times its relativity. What is the full feasible interval for $c$?
options: $200/3\le c\le300$ euros.
$100\le c\le300$ euros.
$100\le c\le200$ euros.
$c=100$ euros only.
